blocks.x: BIOL 151 · Cell Structure · Topic 1

Cells are far too small to see with the naked eye, so almost everything we know about cell structure was learned through microscopes. This topic builds the optics vocabulary and formulas you need before we ever look at an organelle.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Convert between units of microscopic measurement — micrometres (µm), nanometres (nm) and Angstroms (Å) — and express cell and organelle sizes correctly.

2Describe simple microscopes and their history, including Robert Hooke's coining of "cell" and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's discovery of "animalcules," and explain spherical and chromatic aberration and how each is corrected.
3Identify the parts of a compound microscope and a dissecting microscope, and explain the parfocal property and working distance.
4Distinguish magnification from resolution, and explain why increasing magnification beyond ~2000x reveals no new detail.
5Apply the Numerical Aperture and Resolving Power formulas (NA = n sin U; R = 0.61λ/NA) to explain why immersion oil and shorter wavelengths sharpen the image.

blocks.x: Key definitions
Micrometre (µm) 10⁻⁶ m (one millionth of a metre). The standard unit for describing whole cells — a typical animal cell is roughly 10–30 µm across.
Nanometre (nm) 10⁻⁹ m (one billionth of a metre; 1 µm = 1000 nm). Used for organelles, membranes and viruses, which are too small to conveniently express in µm.
Angstrom (Å) 10⁻¹⁰ m (1 nm = 10 Å). Used for atomic and molecular-scale dimensions, such as the diameter of a DNA double helix (~20 Å).

Magnification vs. Resolution Magnification is the apparent increase in the size of an object, and depends on the focal length of the lenses used. Resolution (resolving power) is the ability of an optical system to distinguish two very close points as two separate entities, rather than one blur.
Units of Measurement→ Simple Microscopes & Lens Defects→ Compound Microscope Structure→ Magnification vs Resolution→ Numerical Aperture & Formulas
Where microscopy began

Before compound instruments existed, a single curved piece of glass opened the door to the cellular world. Every simple lens, however, has built-in optical flaws that had to be understood and corrected.
The pioneers of microscopy

Simple microscope An instrument that magnifies using a single lens (a single converging surface), such as a magnifying glass or hand lens/loupe. It is the simplest way to enlarge the apparent size of a small object.

items: RHRobert Hooke (1665) — used a compound microscope of his own design to examine a thin slice of cork. He observed small box-like compartments and named them "cells," because they reminded him of the small rooms (cellulae) that monks lived in. He was actually looking at the empty cell walls of dead plant tissue, not living cells.

ALAntonie van Leeuwenhoek — a Dutch tradesman who ground his own tiny, powerful single-lens (simple) microscopes. He was the first person to observe and describe living microorganisms, which he called "animalcules" — including bacteria and protozoa — opening up the study of microbial life.

blocks.x:
Loupe / hand lens
A simple magnifier consisting of a single small convex lens, held close to the eye, used for quick low-magnification inspection (e.g. of gems, print, or specimens in the field). It is the direct modern descendant of van Leeuwenhoek's simple microscopes.
Lens defects (aberrations)
A single spherical lens is never a perfect image-former. Two aberrations matter most for microscopy: spherical aberration and chromatic aberration.
Spherical aberration

Light rays passing through the edges of a spherical lens are bent (refracted) more strongly than rays passing through its centre. The two sets of rays therefore focus at different points along the axis, so the image is blurred rather than sharply focused.
Chromatic aberration

White light is a mixture of wavelengths (colours), and a simple lens refracts each wavelength by a different amount (shorter wavelengths bend more). The colours therefore focus at slightly different points, producing coloured fringes around the image.
Correcting each aberration

items: 1Correcting spherical aberration: use only the central part of the lens by inserting a diaphragm/stop that blocks the outer rays; use oil immersion to keep rays travelling in a narrower, more uniform path; or use a compound system of several lens elements (including aspherical surfaces) that are shaped to cancel out the focusing error.

2Correcting chromatic aberration: use an achromatic lens — most commonly an achromatic doublet, which cements together a converging lens of crown glass and a diverging lens of flint glass. Because the two glass types have different refractive indices and dispersion properties, their combined effect brings two wavelengths of light (typically red and blue) to a common focus, greatly reducing colour fringing.

blocks.x: Achromatic doublet A compound lens made of crown glass (low dispersion) cemented to flint glass (high dispersion), each with a different refractive index. This combination corrects chromatic aberration and is the basis of the "achromat" objectives found on most compound microscopes.

blocks.title: Why does this matter for cell biology?

items: An uncorrected simple lens gives a blurred, colour-fringed image — useless for distinguishing fine cellular detail.

Every modern compound microscope objective (achromat, fluorite, apochromat — covered later in this topic) is really a carefully engineered multi-element lens system built to minimise both spherical and chromatic aberration at once.
Better correction of aberrations is one reason apochromat objectives cost more and give crisper images than plain achromats, even at the same magnification.

sections.title: How light travels through the instrument

blocks.x: Two lenses working together
The compound microscope multiplies magnification by combining two lens systems in series, and adds a whole support structure — stage, condenser, focus knobs — to make that magnification usable.

Compound microscope A microscope with two magnifying lens systems arranged along one optical path: the ocular (eyepiece) lens, closest to the observer's eye, and the objective lens, closest to the specimen. Total magnification = eyepiece power × objective power.
How light travels through the instrument
Light Source→ Condenser→ Specimen→ Objective Lens→ Eyepiece (Ocular)→ Eye
Key parts of a compound microscope

items: 1Eyepiece (ocular lens): the lens you look through, typically 10x or 15x magnifying power.
2Nosepiece: the rotating turret that holds the objective lenses and lets you click between them.
3Objective lenses: mounted on the nosepiece, typically in a set of low power, high power, and oil-immersion objectives, each with a different magnification and numerical aperture.
4Stage: the flat platform that holds the specimen slide in the light path.
5Condenser: a lens beneath the stage that focuses/concentrates light from the source onto the specimen.

6Iris diaphragm: an adjustable aperture (usually part of, or just below, the condenser) that controls how much light and how wide a cone of light reaches the specimen, affecting contrast and numerical aperture.
7Coarse and fine focus knobs: the coarse knob moves the stage/objective quickly for initial focusing; the fine knob makes small, precise adjustments for a sharp image.
8Light source: illuminates the specimen from below, typically an integrated lamp or mirror.

blocks.x: Parfocal property & working distance

Parfocal A microscope is parfocal when the image stays approximately in focus as you rotate the nosepiece from one objective to another (e.g. from 10x to 40x). Only minor fine-focus adjustment is then needed, which is why you should always start focusing on the lowest power objective.

Working distance The physical gap between the tip of the objective lens and the surface of the specimen when the image is in focus. Working distance decreases as objective magnification increases — the high-power and oil-immersion objectives sit very close to (and for oil immersion, are optically linked by oil to) the slide.
The dissecting (stereo) microscope

Dissecting / stereo microscope Designed for low magnification (roughly up to 30x) viewing of larger or opaque specimens (e.g. insects, flowers, dissections) that cannot be flattened onto a slide. It uses two separate optical paths, one for each eye, giving a true 3-D (stereoscopic) view rather than the flat image of a compound microscope.

blocks.title: Compound vs. dissecting microscope — quick comparison

items: Compound microscope: single optical path split to two eyepieces, high magnification (up to ~2000x with oil), specimen must be thin/translucent and mounted on a slide, image is 2-D.
Dissecting microscope: two independent optical paths, low magnification (up to ~30x), specimen can be thick/opaque and viewed whole, image is 3-D.

sections.title: How far can a light microscope go?

blocks.x: Bigger is not always better
A photo can be zoomed in endlessly on a screen, but past a certain point it just gets blurrier, not more detailed. Microscopes have the same limit — and it's set by resolution, not magnification.

Magnification The apparent increase in the size of an object as seen through the instrument, compared with its actual size. It depends on the focal length of the lenses in the system (eyepiece power × objective power for a compound microscope).

Resolution (resolving power) The ability of an optical system to distinguish two points that are very close together as two separate entities rather than a single blurred point. Resolution is what actually determines how much genuine detail an image can show.
How far can a light microscope go?

25–1500xtypical magnification range of an ordinary glass compound microscope ~2000xmaximum useful magnification achievable with an oil-immersion objective >2000x"empty magnification" — the image gets bigger but reveals no new detail

Empty magnification Magnifying an image beyond the resolution limit of the optical system (roughly beyond 2000x for a light microscope). The image becomes larger and blurrier, but no additional fine detail becomes visible, because resolution — not magnification — sets the ceiling on how much detail can ever be seen.
Resolution is a physical, not an engineering, limit

Because light behaves as a wave, there is a fundamental physical limit to how finely a lens can distinguish two close points — this limit does not disappear just because you add stronger eyepieces or more magnifying lenses. The theoretical best-case resolving power of a light microscope is approximately:

Theoretical maximal resolving power r = λ / 2 — where λ is the wavelength of light used. For green light (λ ≈ 600 nm, roughly 560 nm being the wavelength the human eye is most sensitive to), this gives a theoretical best resolution of about 280–300 nm.

In practice, real resolving power also depends on the numerical aperture of the lens system (covered fully in the next tab) — but the core idea is the same: two structures closer together than this limit will always appear as one blurred structure, no matter how much you magnify the image.

items: Switching from a 10x to a 40x objective and the image simply gets bigger with no new detail visible → you have hit the resolution limit; further magnification is "empty."
Two adjacent mitochondria that were a single blur at 1000x become two distinct blobs at 2000x with oil immersion → this is genuinely improved resolution, not just magnification.
Zooming into a photo on your phone past its pixel limit → a everyday analogy for "empty magnification."

blocks.x: The maths behind sharpness

Two formulas govern everything about how sharp a microscope image can be: Numerical Aperture (NA) and Resolving Power (R). Together they explain why immersion oil is used and why shorter-wavelength light gives crisper images.
Numerical Aperture (NA)

NA = n sin U n = refractive index of the medium between the objective lens and the specimen (air, water, glycerin or oil). U = half of the angular aperture — half the angle of the cone of light rays that enters the objective lens from the specimen. A higher NA means the objective can gather a wider cone of light and resolve finer detail.
Resolving Power (R)

R = 0.61λ / NA λ = wavelength of the light used to illuminate the specimen. NA = numerical aperture of the objective lens. R is the minimum distance between two points that the microscope can still show as separate — the smaller R is, the better (finer) the resolution.

Reading the formula: R gets smaller (resolution improves) when λ decreases (shorter-wavelength/bluer light) or when NA increases. This is why microscopists chase the shortest practical wavelength and the highest achievable NA.
Immersion oil and refractive index

Since NA = n sin U, increasing the refractive index n of the medium between the specimen and the objective directly increases NA — and therefore improves resolution (shrinks R). Air has a low refractive index and also causes light rays at wide angles to refract away from the objective and be lost. Immersion oil is chosen to closely match the refractive index of glass, so light rays pass from the slide into the objective with far less bending and loss, capturing a wider effective cone of light (larger U) at a higher n.
Refractive index (n) of common media

Immersion oil's refractive index is often quoted as approximately 1.51–1.55, closely matching the refractive index of glass — this is what lets it minimise refraction losses at the slide-to-objective interface.
Numerical aperture across objective types

Different objective lens designs correct aberrations to different degrees, and this is reflected in their NA at a given magnification — better-corrected, more expensive objectives (fluorite, then apochromat) achieve a higher NA than a basic achromat at the same power.
Putting the formulas together
A Plan Fluorite 40x oil-immersion objective has NA = 1.30. Using green light (λ = 550 nm), estimate the resolving power R.

items: 1Write the resolving power formula and identify the values.R = 0.61λ / NA, λ = 550 nm, NA = 1.30
2Substitute the values.R = 0.61 × 550 / 1.30 = 335.5 / 1.30
3Divide to find R.R ≈ 258 nm

blocks.x: Answer: R ≈ 258 nm — two points closer together than this will appear as one blur, even under oil immersion.

items: Decrease λ — use shorter-wavelength (bluer/UV) light → R gets smaller (better resolution).
Increase NA — use a higher-NA objective (apochromat over achromat) and/or immersion oil (raises n) → R gets smaller.
Increasing magnification alone, without changing λ or NA, does not improve resolution — it only risks "empty magnification."
